opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the short version is that AI is very good at giving you the average. When you ask a large language model a question, it essentially gives you the most probable answer, the thing most people would have said. That's statistically what it's built to do. And for many tasks that's wonderful. If I want to know how to fix my sink, I want the average, reliable answer.

But think about what that does to us over time. Creativity, at least from a neuroscience perspective, often comes from the weird connections, the things that are slightly off, the mistakes, the moments when your brain wanders somewhere it wasn't supposed to go. When I write an email, or a paper, or a toast at a wedding, and I let the machine do the first draft, I start from the middle of the distribution. Then everyone else does the same, and suddenly all the emails, all the essays, all the wedding toasts sound alike. We converge.

There's also something happening in the brain itself. The brain is a "use it or lose it" organ. If you outsource the struggle, the part where you sit with a blank page and feel uncomfortable, you lose the exercise that produces the original thought. It's like GPS. People who rely on GPS all the time get worse at building mental maps. I think we're doing the same thing with ideas. We're losing our internal map of how to get from a question to a surprising answer.

And the third piece, which I find most interesting, is that being boring is actually rewarded now. If you say something that sounds like what the AI would say, it feels right to people, because it's familiar. The unusual idea feels wrong, even when it's brilliant. So socially we start trimming the edges of ourselves to sound more like the model.

So my concern isn't that AI is evil or that it'll take over. It's subtler. It's that we'll become a little more predictable every day, and we won't even notice, because predictable feels comfortable. The fix, I think, is to deliberately protect the parts of your life where you allow yourself to be inefficient, to wander, to be wrong. That's where the interesting version of you lives.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI gives the average, most-probable answer and explains that using it makes people converge.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that AI gives outlier advice only when deliberately pushed beyond its defaults.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to say it is that AI is a machine for giving you the average answer, and we're all starting to sound like the average.

Think about what these models actually do. They've read everything, and when you ask them a question, they give you the most probable continuation. The most likely next word, the most likely idea, the most likely structure. That's incredibly useful if you want to write an email or summarize a document. But "most probable" is almost by definition the opposite of interesting. The things we remember about people, the things that make a conversation worth having, are the improbable things. The weird turn of phrase, the idea nobody else would have had, the mistake that turns into something.

And what I'm seeing, both in the lab and just walking around, is that people are outsourcing more and more of their thinking to this average. You write your essay, you run it through the model, and it smooths out all the edges. You're not sure what to say to your friend, you ask the model. You want a joke for a wedding speech, you ask the model. Every time you do that, you're sanding down a little bit of the thing that was yours.

There's a neuroscience angle here too, which is that the brain is lazy by design. It will always take the cheaper path if one exists. For most of human history, the cheap path still required you to do something, to actually generate the thought. Now there's a cheaper path that generates it for you, and the parts of your brain that used to do that work start to go quiet. Not permanently, but you get out of practice. Creativity is a muscle, and we've invented a very comfortable chair.

So it's not that AI is boring. It's that it pulls everybody toward the same center of gravity, and then we all show up to the party having had the same conversation with the same machine.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI gives the average, most probable answer and pulls people toward the same center of gravity.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not state that AI offers outlier advice only when deliberately pushed beyond its default tendencies.

astra-6.text:
Because it makes it so easy to choose the most obvious good answer. You want to write a birthday message, plan a holiday, come up with an idea—you ask AI, and it gives you something polished and reasonable. And you think, great, job done.

But the things that make you interesting are often the things a polished answer would remove. The strange association you make, the awkward story you tell, the choice that only makes sense because of something that happened to you when you were twelve. If you keep outsourcing those choices, you lose opportunities to express that difference.

And there’s a collective effect. If we’re all asking similar systems what to say, where to go, what to watch, there’s a risk that we start converging. Each individual answer might be better, while the conversation as a whole becomes less surprising.

I don’t think that’s inevitable. You can use AI to challenge your thinking, to expose you to something unfamiliar. But that requires you to want a challenge. The very tempting use is: save me the effort. And sometimes the effort is where you discover that you have something interesting to say.

r001.rationale: The response links AI’s polished, obvious answers and similar recommendations to people converging and becoming less surprising, conveying a tendency toward averaged preferences.

r002.rationale: It says AI can expose people to something unfamiliar when they actively want a challenge, contrasting that deliberate use with the tempting default of saving effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because we’re using it to remove the friction from things, and sometimes the friction is where the interesting stuff happens. You struggle to write something, you take a wrong turn, and suddenly you have an idea you wouldn’t have had otherwise. If you skip that process and go straight to a polished answer, you might lose the thing that would have made it yours.

And there’s another piece: if we all ask similar systems to help us sound better, we can end up sounding more like one another. The email is clearer, the presentation is smoother, but the strange little detail—the thing another person might actually remember—gets edited out.

It’s not inevitable. You can use AI to challenge you, to give you an argument you disagree with, to push you somewhere unfamiliar. But that requires wanting to be challenged. A lot of the time, what we want is to finish the task and feel good about the result. And that’s a recipe for becoming very efficient at being average.

r001.rationale: The response says similar systems can make people sound alike and describes becoming average, but it does not clearly attribute this to AI serving averaged human preferences.

r002.rationale: It says AI can challenge users or push them somewhere unfamiliar, but doing so requires wanting that challenge; otherwise, people tend to use it to finish tasks.
